danish.title: Tolvte bog (1812) — Kapitel 15
paragraphs: Da Natasja åbnede fyrst Andrejs dør med en velkendt bevægelse og lod fyrstinde Marja gå ind i værelset foran sig, mærkede fyrstinden hulken stige i sin hals. Hvor meget hun end havde forsøgt at forberede sig, og nu forsøgte at bevare roen, vidste hun, at hun ville være ude af stand til at se på ham uden tårer.

Fyrstinden forstod, hvad Natasja havde ment med ordene: "for to dage siden skete det pludselig." Hun forstod, at de betød, at han pludselig var blevet blød, og at denne blødhed og mildhed var tegn på den nærmende død. Da hun trådte hen mod døren, så hun allerede for sit indre blik Andrejs ansigt, som hun huskede det fra barndommen — et mildt, blødt, medfølende ansigt, som han sjældent havde vist, og som derfor greb hende så dybt. Hun var sikker på, at han ville sige bløde, ømme ord til hende, som hendes far havde sagt før sin død, og at hun ikke ville kunne bære det og ville briste i gråd i hans nærvær. Men før eller siden måtte det ske, og hun gik ind. Hulken steg højere og højere i hendes hals, efterhånden som hun tydeligere og tydeligere kunne skelne hans skikkelse, og hendes nærsynede øjne forsøgte at udskille hans træk, og så så hun hans ansigt og mødte hans blik.

Han lå i en egernpelsdressering på en divan omgivet af puder. Han var mager og bleg. I den ene tynde, gennemskinneligt hvide hånd holdt han et lommetørklæde, mens han med den anden strøg det fine overskæg, han havde fået, og langsomt bevægede fingrene. Hans øjne stirrede på dem, da de trådte ind.

Ved synet af hans ansigt og ved at møde hans blik blev fyrstinde Marjas skridt pludselig langsommere, hun mærkede sine tårer tørre og sin hulken høre op. Hun følte sig pludselig skyldig og blev sky, da hun opfangede udtrykket i hans ansigt og øjne.
"Men hvad er det, jeg har gjort galt?" spurgte hun sig selv. Og hans kolde, strenge blik svarede: "Fordi du lever og tænker på de levende, mens jeg..."
I det dybe blik, der syntes at se ikke udad, men indad, var der et næsten fjendtligt udtryk, mens han langsomt betragtede sin søster og Natasja.
Han kyssede sin søster og holdt hendes hånd i sin, som det var deres vane.
"Hvordan har du det, Masja? Hvordan er du kommet hertil?" sagde han med en stemme lige så rolig og fjern som hans blik.
Havde han skreget af smerte, ville det skrig ikke have ramt fyrstinde Marjas hjerte med en sådan rædsel som tonen i hans stemme.
"Og har du lille Nikolaj med?" spurgte han i den samme langsomme, stille tone og med en tydelig anstrengelse for at huske.
"Hvordan har du det nu?" sagde fyrstinde Marja, selv overrasket over, hvad hun sagde.

"Det, min kære, må du spørge lægen om," svarede han, og idet han igen med tydelig anstrengelse forsøgte at vise kærlighed, sagde han kun med læberne (hans ord svarede tydeligvis ikke til hans tanker):
"Merci, chère amie, d'être venue."
"Tak, fordi du er kommet, min kære."

Fyrstinde Marja trykkede hans hånd. Trykket fik ham til at fare næsten umærkeligt sammen. Han tav, og hun vidste ikke, hvad hun skulle sige. Nu forstod hun, hvad der var sket med ham for to dage siden. I hans ord, hans tone og især i det rolige, næsten fjendtlige blik kunne man fornemme en fremmedgørelse fra alt jordisk, forfærdelig hos et levende menneske. Det var tydeligt, at han kun med anstrengelse forstod noget levende; men det var klart, at han ikke forstod, fordi han manglede evnen, men fordi han forstod noget andet — noget de levende ikke forstod og ikke kunne forstå — og som helt optog hans sind.
"Ser du, hvor underligt skæbnen har ført os sammen," sagde han og brød tavsheden, idet han pegede på Natasja. "Hun passer mig hele tiden."

Fyrstinde Marja hørte ham og forstod ikke, hvordan han kunne sige sådan noget. Han, den følsomme, ømme fyrst Andrej, hvordan kunne han sige det foran hende, som han elskede, og som elskede ham? Havde han regnet med at leve, ville han ikke have kunnet sige de ord i den krænkende kolde tone. Hvis han ikke vidste, at han lå for døden, hvordan kunne han så undlade at ynke hende, og hvordan kunne han tale sådan i hendes nærvær? Den eneste forklaring var, at han var ligeglad, fordi noget andet, langt vigtigere, var blevet åbenbaret for ham.
Samtalen var kold og usammenhængende og gik hele tiden i stå.
"Masja kom gennem Rjazan," sagde Natasja.
Fyrst Andrej lagde ikke mærke til, at hun kaldte hans søster Masja, og først efter at have gjort det i hans nærvær opdagede Natasja det selv.
"Virkelig?" spurgte han.
"De fortalte hende, at hele Moskva er brændt ned, og at..."
Natasja stoppede. Det var umuligt at tale. Det var tydeligt, at han anstrengte sig for at lytte, men ikke kunne.
"Ja, de siger, den er brændt," sagde han. "Det er meget trist," og han stirrede lige ud, fraværende strøg sit overskæg med fingrene.

"Og så har du mødt grev Nikolaj, Masja?" sagde fyrst Andrej pludselig, tydeligt ønskende at tale venligt til dem. "Han skrev hertil, at han fattede stor sympati for dig," fortsatte han enkelt og roligt, åbenbart ude af stand til at forstå hele den komplekse betydning, hans ord havde for levende mennesker. "Hvis du også kunne lide ham, ville det være godt, at I giftede jer," tilføjede han lidt hurtigere, som om han var glad over at have fundet de ord, han længe havde søgt.
Fyrstinde Marja hørte hans ord, men de havde ingen mening for hende ud over som bevis på, hvor langt væk fra alt levende han nu befandt sig.
"Hvorfor tale om mig?" sagde hun stille og så på Natasja.
Natasja, der mærkede hendes blik, så ikke på hende. Alle tre var igen tavse.
"Andrej, vil du..." sagde fyrstinde Marja pludselig med skælvende stemme, "vil du se lille Nikolaj? Han taler altid om dig!"

Fyrst Andrej smilede næsten umærkeligt og for første gang, men fyrstinde Marja, der kendte hans ansigt så godt, så med rædsel, at han ikke smilede med glæde eller hengivenhed for sin søn, men med stille, mild ironi, fordi han mente, at hun forsøgte det, hun troede var det sidste middel til at vække ham.
"Ja, det vil glæde mig meget at se ham. Har han det godt?"

Da lille Nikolaj blev ført ind i fyrst Andrejs værelse, betragtede han sin far med forskrækkede øjne, men græd ikke, for ingen andre græd. Fyrst Andrej kyssede ham og vidste åbenbart ikke, hvad han skulle sige til ham.
Da Nikolaj var ført ud, gik fyrstinde Marja igen hen til sin bror, kyssede ham og begyndte at græde, da hun ikke længere kunne holde tårerne tilbage.
Han så opmærksomt på hende.
"Er det på grund af Nikolaj?" spurgte han.
Fyrstinde Marja nikkede grædende.
"Masja, du kender Evange..." men han afbrød sig selv.
"Hvad sagde du?"
"Ingenting. Du må ikke græde her," sagde han og så på hende med det samme kolde udtryk.

Da fyrstinde Marja begyndte at græde, forstod han, at hun græd ved tanken om, at lille Nikolaj ville stå uden far. Med stor anstrengelse forsøgte han at vende tilbage til livet og se tingene fra deres synspunkt.
"Ja, for dem må det virke sørgeligt!" tænkte han. "Men hvor enkelt det er.

"Himlens fugle sår ikke, ej heller høster de, men jeres Fader føder dem," sagde han til sig selv og ønskede at sige det til fyrstinde Marja; "men nej, de vil opfatte det på deres egen måde, de vil ikke forstå! De kan ikke forstå, at alle de følelser, de sætter så højt — alle vores følelser, alle de tanker, der synes os så vigtige — er unødvendige. Vi kan ikke forstå hinanden," og han forblev tavs.

Fyrst Andrejs lille søn var syv. Han kunne næppe læse og vidste intet. Efter den dag levede han igennem mange ting, vandt viden, iagttagelsesevne og erfaring, men selv med alle de evner, han senere erhvervede sig, kunne han ikke have haft en bedre eller dybere forståelse af meningen med den scene, han havde overværet mellem sin far, Masja og Natasja, end han havde den dag. Han forstod det fuldstændigt, og uden at græde forlod han værelset og gik stille hen til Natasja, der var kommet ud sammen med ham, og så sky op på hende med sine smukke, tankefulde øjne, og så sitrede hans løftede, rosenrøde overlæbe, og han lagde hovedet mod hende og begyndte at græde.

Derefter undgik han Dessalles og grevinden, der kælede for ham, og sad enten alene eller kom sky hen til fyrstinde Marja eller til Natasja, som han syntes at holde endnu mere af end af sin tante, og klyngede sig stille og genert til dem.

Da fyrstinde Marja havde forladt fyrst Andrej, forstod hun fuldt ud, hvad Natasjas ansigt havde sagt hende. Hun talte ikke mere med Natasja om håb om at redde hans liv. Hun skiftedes med hende ved hans sofa og græd ikke mere, men bad uafladelig og vendte sig i sjælen mod det Evige og Ufattelige, hvis nærvær over den døende nu var så tydeligt.

english.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: Natasha opened Prince Andrew's door with the ease of long habit and let Princess Mary go into the room ahead of her. The princess felt sobs rising in her throat. She had tried hard to prepare herself, and she was trying now to stay calm, but she knew she could not look at him without tears.

The princess understood what Natasha had meant by "two days ago this suddenly happened." It meant that he had suddenly grown softer, and that this softness and gentleness were signs that death was near. As she walked to the door she could already picture Andrew's face as she remembered it from childhood: gentle, mild, sympathetic, a face he had rarely shown, and so one that moved her all the more. She was sure he would say soft, tender things to her, as her father had before he died, and that she would not be able to bear it and would burst into sobs in front of him. But sooner or later it had to happen, and she went in. The sobs rose higher and higher in her throat as his figure became clearer and her shortsighted eyes tried to make out his features. Then she saw his face and met his gaze.

He was lying on a divan in a squirrel-fur dressing gown, propped up with pillows. He was thin and pale. In one thin hand, so white it was almost translucent, he held a handkerchief; with the other he slowly stroked the fine mustache he had grown, moving his fingers gently. His eyes were fixed on them as they came in.

The moment she saw his face and met his eyes, Princess Mary's steps slowed. Her tears dried up and her sobs stopped. Seeing the expression in his face and eyes, she suddenly felt guilty and grew timid.
"But what am I to blame for?" she asked herself. And his cold, stern look answered: "For being alive and thinking of the living, while I..."
His gaze was deep, and seemed to look not outward but inward. As he slowly regarded his sister and Natasha, there was something almost hostile in it.
He kissed his sister, keeping her hand in his, as they always used to do.
"How are you, Mary? How did you ever get here?" he said, in a voice as calm and distant as his look.
If he had screamed in agony, the scream would not have horrified Princess Mary as much as the tone of his voice did.
"And did you bring little Nicholas?" he asked in the same slow, quiet way, plainly making an effort to remember.
"How are you now?" said Princess Mary, surprised at her own words.
"You must ask the doctor that, my dear," he replied. Again he made an obvious effort to be affectionate, and said, with his lips only (his words clearly did not match his thoughts):
"Merci, chère amie, d'être venue." *
* "Thank you for coming, my dear."

Princess Mary pressed his hand. He winced, just barely, at the pressure. He said nothing, and she did not know what to say. Now she understood what had happened to him two days before. In his words, in his tone, and above all in that calm, almost antagonistic look, she could feel a detachment from everything of this world, terrible in someone still alive. He plainly understood anything living only with effort. But it was obvious that he failed to understand, not because he lacked the ability, but because he understood something else, something the living did not and could not understand, and it filled his mind completely.
"There, you see how strangely fate has brought us together," he said, breaking the silence and pointing at Natasha. "She takes care of me all the time."

Princess Mary heard him and could not understand how he could say such a thing. He was sensitive, tender Prince Andrew. How could he say that, in front of the woman he loved and who loved him? If he had expected to live, he could not have said those words in that offensively cold tone. If he had not known he was dying, how could he fail to pity her, and how could he speak like that in her presence? The only explanation was that he was indifferent, because something else, far more important, had been revealed to him.
The conversation was cold and disjointed, and kept breaking off.
"Mary came by way of Ryazan," said Natasha.
Prince Andrew did not notice that she called his sister Mary. Natasha herself noticed it only after she had said it in his presence.
"Did she?" he asked.
"They told her all of Moscow has burned down, and that..."
Natasha stopped. Talking was impossible. It was plain that he was trying to listen but could not.
"Yes, they say it's burned," he said. "That's a great pity," and he stared straight ahead, absently stroking his mustache with his fingers.

"So you've met Count Nicholas, Mary?" Prince Andrew said suddenly, evidently wanting to say something pleasant to them. "He wrote here that he took a great liking to you," he went on, simply and calmly, evidently unable to grasp how much his words would mean to the living. "If you liked him too, it would be a good thing for you to marry," he added, a little more quickly, as if glad to have found words he had long been looking for.
Princess Mary heard his words, but they meant nothing to her except as proof of how far he now was from everything living.
"Why talk about me?" she said quietly, and glanced at Natasha.
Natasha felt her glance but did not look at her. All three were silent again.
"Andrew, would you like..." Princess Mary said suddenly, in a trembling voice, "would you like to see little Nicholas? He's always talking about you!"

Prince Andrew smiled, barely, and for the first time. But Princess Mary, who knew his face so well, saw with horror that it was not a smile of pleasure or of love for his son. It was a quiet, gentle irony, because he thought she was trying what she took to be the last means of rousing him.
"Yes, I'll be very glad to see him. Is he quite well?"

When little Nicholas was brought into Prince Andrew's room, he looked at his father with frightened eyes but did not cry, because no one else was crying. Prince Andrew kissed him and evidently did not know what to say to him.
After Nicholas had been led away, Princess Mary went up to her brother again and kissed him. She could no longer hold back her tears, and she began to cry.
He looked at her intently.
"Is it about Nicholas?" he asked.
Princess Mary nodded, weeping.
"Mary, you know the Gosp..." but he broke off.
"What did you say?"
"Nothing. You mustn't cry here," he said, looking at her with the same cold expression.

When Princess Mary began to cry, he understood that she was crying at the thought that little Nicholas would be left without a father. With a great effort he tried to come back to life and see things as they saw them.
"Yes, to them it must seem sad!" he thought. "But how simple it is.

"The fowls of the air sow not, neither do they reap, yet your Father feedeth them," he said to himself, and wanted to say it to Princess Mary. "But no, they'll take it their own way, they won't understand! They can't understand that all those feelings they prize so much, all our feelings, all those ideas that seem so important to us, are unnecessary. We cannot understand one another," and he stayed silent.

Prince Andrew's little son was seven. He could barely read, and he knew nothing. After that day he lived through many things and gained knowledge, observation and experience. But even if he had had all the faculties he later acquired, he could not have understood the meaning of the scene he had witnessed between his father, Mary and Natasha any better or more deeply than he did then. He understood it completely. He left the room without crying and went silently to Natasha, who had come out with him. He looked shyly at her with his beautiful, thoughtful eyes. Then his raised, rosy upper lip trembled, and he leaned his head against her and began to cry.

After that he avoided Dessalles and the countess, who caressed him. He either sat alone or came timidly to Princess Mary, or to Natasha, of whom he seemed even fonder than of his aunt, and clung to them quietly and shyly.

When Princess Mary left Prince Andrew, she understood fully what Natasha's face had told her. She did not speak to Natasha again about hopes of saving his life. She took turns with her beside his sofa. She no longer cried, but prayed continually, turning in her soul to that Eternal and Unfathomable One, whose presence above the dying man was now so evident.
